summary: This memo defines one authentication protocol and one privacy protocol for SNMPv2 so management messages can be authenticated and encrypted. It is historic.

eli5.summary: This paper describes how to prove a network management message is real and keep it secret from snoopers. It is historic.

questions: what is the digest authentication protocol
subtitle: Authentication and encryption for network management messages

tldr.problem: Network management systems need to authenticate that management commands come from authorized sources and encrypt sensitive network information from eavesdropping.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1446 defines two protocols: a digest authentication protocol using MD5 to verify message origin and integrity, and a symmetric privacy protocol using DES encryption to protect message contents.
tldr.outcome: These security mechanisms were used in early SNMPv2 deployments but the standard is now historic, replaced by later SNMPv3 security frameworks.

today: RFC 1445 (SNMPv2 administrative model) that defines parties using these protocols is now historic. SNMPv3 (RFC 3410 and related RFCs) superseded SNMPv2 with a different user and security model that does not use parties.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Network management systems send commands from management stations to agents on network devices like routers and switches. These commands control and monitor the network, so they must be protected from two kinds of attack: someone impersonating a manager to issue unauthorized commands, and someone eavesdropping on management traffic to learn network secrets.

RFC 1446 defines two security protocols that work together in SNMPv2. The Digest Authentication Protocol proves that a message really came from who it claims to be and that it was not altered in transit. The Symmetric Privacy Protocol encrypts the message so only the intended recipient can read it. Both protocols are used together; a message cannot be encrypted without first being authenticated.
sections.eli5: A manager has to prove they really are the boss before the router listens to them. And if the command is really secret, the router needs to scramble it so hackers cannot read it on the wire.

sections.title: Parties and Authentication Information
sections.content:
In SNMPv2, each entity (a management station or a network agent) takes on the role of a party, which is a conceptual identity that is associated with specific authentication and privacy settings. Each party stores a private authentication key and a private privacy key. These keys are known only to the two parties that communicate with each other.

An authenticated message carries authentication information in addition to the management command. This includes an authentication digest (computed from the message and the secret key), an authentication timestamp from the sender, and a destination timestamp from the receiver. The timestamps protect against replay attacks where an attacker replays an old message to repeat a command.
sections.eli5: Each manager and router has a secret password that only the two of them know. Every message includes a special number (a digest) that proves the password was used, plus time stamps so old messages cannot be played back.

sections.title: Digest Authentication Protocol
sections.content:
The Digest Authentication Protocol uses the MD5 message digest algorithm. To send an authenticated message, the originator looks up its private authentication key and the current time on its authentication clock. It also learns the receiver's authentication clock time. It then computes a digest by prefixing the private key to the message, serializing it, and running it through the MD5 algorithm. The result is included in the message along with both clock values.

To receive an authenticated message, the recipient checks that the sender's timestamp is within an acceptable lifetime window to prevent old replayed messages. It reconstructs what the digest should be by prefixing the sender's private key to the received message and running MD5. If the computed digest matches the received digest, the message is authentic. If it does not match, the message is discarded and an error counter is incremented. Once a message is authentic, the recipient advances its own clock values if the received timestamps are newer.
sections.eli5: To send a message, the manager mixes its secret password with the command, runs it through a special code-making machine, and sends the code along with the message. The router mixes the same password with the message and runs it through the code-making machine. If it gets the same code, the message is real.

sections.title: Symmetric Privacy Protocol
sections.content:
The Symmetric Privacy Protocol uses the Data Encryption Standard (DES) algorithm in Cipher Block Chaining mode to encrypt the authenticated message. The protocol assumes the underlying mechanism is a symmetric encryption algorithm where both parties have the same secret key. For DES, the private privacy key is 16 octets: the first 8 octets are the 56-bit DES key (plus 8 parity bits), and the second 8 octets are the DES initialization vector.

The message to be encrypted is the serialized authenticated message itself, which already contains the authentication digest. The encryption takes place after authentication, so privacy always depends on having authentication as well. The data being encrypted must be padded to a multiple of 8 octets to meet DES requirements. After decryption, the padding is discarded.
sections.eli5: If the message is really secret, the manager scrambles the whole authenticated message using a secret code that only the router knows. The router unscrambles it to read the message. The scrambling happens after the proof-of-identity part.

sections.title: Threats and Design Goals
sections.content:
The RFC addresses several key threats to network management. The modification threat is the danger that an attacker can alter a message to cause unauthorized management operations. The masquerade threat is that an attacker can assume the identity of an authorized manager to issue commands. The disclosure threat is that sensitive management information might be eavesdropped on, which is especially critical when new parties are being configured. The RFC also identifies message stream modification (replay or reordering of messages) as a secondary threat that must be defended against.

The design explicitly does not attempt to protect against denial-of-service attacks or traffic analysis, as these are difficult to defend against in a connectionless protocol and often indistinguishable from normal network failures. The use of loose clock synchronization and secret keys eliminates the need for external services like NTP, keeping the security mechanism independent and manageable.
sections.eli5: Attackers might change a command to say the wrong thing, pretend to be a real manager, snoop on secrets, or replay old commands. The protocols stop most of these. They do not try to stop someone jamming the network or counting how many commands get sent, since those are too hard.
